stories.title_en: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp

comments.author: rao-v
comments.text:
Early in 2025 a bunch of folks realized that AMD made a bunch of cards with mediocre compute but incredibly fast HBM2 memory in their circa 2018 gfx906 datacenter series, so you could get 32GB VRAM capable of incredible 1 TB / s bandwidth for $200 (the closest in today’s cards is north of $3000)
There has been a rich little ecosystem of folks optimizing llama.cpp for these odd cards (no tensor cores, no native bf16 etc.) including my little personal repo
https://github.com/kinchahoy/llama-of-vega.cpp
. Stuff like this focused on more modern RDNA doesn’t help us at all.
It’s been interesting to see how much each new frontier model can figure out in terms of optimizing for these GPUs and what they can’t!
Fable and Astra will regularly run out of ideas until I point them to someone’s actually thoughtful repo and then they’ll diligently incorporate ideas.
The optimization wins are huge (I was initially skeptical that per model kernel optimizations would be worth much). 27B at a pristine Q8 quant goes from base llama.cpp at some 250 pp / 25 tg to 600 pp / 40 tg even before speculative decoding.

comments.author: malicz
comments.text:
I have a r9700 card and I highly recommend the radiance engine. With a single card it processes (prefill) at 2400 tok/s and decodes at 150 tok/s. With a 4-bit model that is intelligently quantised to have a KLD of 0.006 and top-1 of 0.972
I have been working this engine for a month, throwing a lot of agentic and coding work and it has been doing great! I can run 3 concurrent agent streams all with a 200k context, entirely in vram.
EDIT: model: Qwen3.8-27b -
https://codeberg.org/StillDeadcode/radiance

comments.author: dofm
comments.text:
I saw some blurb a while ago that described llama.cpp as a “model zoo”, which is a great description of its utility and generality.
In the last couple of days I have been playing with Erik Paperniuk’s M1 port of Inco’s Splash, which has completely transformed the speed of Qwen 3.8 27B and Inkling 2 Mini; it has essentially tripled the speed of the former and more than doubled the speed of the latter.
This means the Qwen model is fully viable on an M1 Max, where before I had found it a bit of a waiting game. And it arguably transforms the utility of Inkling 2 Mini; extra speed means it can be left to reason for longer, the downside of needing to do more tool use for search to patch its knowledge is reduced, and it provides a good rough chat model (though this is not its area of greatest strength).
I have not yet found anything that can boost Muse Glimmer to the same extent; I would still prefer that.
But for me I now find that only the rather slow prefill speed really holds the M1 Max back; I suspect these new custom kernels have made the M5 Pro Mac Mini a really cost-effective option if you want to tinker with local AI.

https://github.com/fwoar-greenhouse/vicuna.cpp
I've been running this for a while and it seems pretty stable, plus I had Claude validate the ported kernels against the originals to make sure they were reasonably close numerically to the validated implementations.

stories.title_en: AI made self-hosting fun again

comments.author: jjcm
comments.text:
In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse.
It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end.
The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate.
It got so bad during October I made
https://firefighter.sh/
as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

stories.title_en: George Whitesides, 1939-2026

comments.author: tomwphillips
comments.text:
He spoke at Imperial College London when I was doing my PhD. Sometime between 2011-2015. He spoke about paper based microfluidic devices for rapid medical diagnostic tests. If memory serves he made clear to the audience that his "cheap" devices _were not cheap enough_ to be useful in developing countries. I admired the intellectual rigour and honesty.
It resonated with me as I was part of a doctoral training centre for plastic electronics. Everyone was making these devices using incredibly expensive materials and low throughput techniques, but the only way the technology could be viable commercially was for it to be extremely cheap. IIRC there was one paper that calculated that the devices has to be as cheap as carpet to be worthwhile.
Granted, I was a pretty obnoxious twenty-something, but it didn't make me popular to point this out to my fellow researchers.

comments.author: t3ntxcles

Cool hack, getting fork-per-connection postgres running with no kernel is quite interesting
I'm struggling to see the use case for minipg itself. For embedded or in-process postgres there's pglite as mentioned in comments. For dev/test parity there's embedded-postgres (go, java, node, python), which downloads native binaries and gives you a throwaway postgres with no docker. These by themselves cover what most people would want from "sqlite-style postgres," without the hypervisor layer or significant slow down.

I can see this very useful for small self-hosted applications. I could imagine deploying this instead of sqlite in some cases. Though having a real server is not maybe ideal for self-hosted apps.
For unit tests I've found that I don't need PGLite or other tools, only podman and official images.
Regular postgres starts in 800 milliseconds, TimeScale DB in 1 second.
I have setup where first unit test that starts podman container and after finish it ends it all. On each test I create new database (or search path), time it takes to create db is in milliseconds.

comments.author: progrium
comments.text:
Keep in mind there are two ways to think about SQLite. Most commonly, as these comments show, it's thought of as a library. An embedded SQL engine. The second is as a simple CLI-friendly SQL database. Minipg is more about the latter use.
That said, PGlite is great and would have been ideal for the motivating problem, but as my blog post mentions (eventually), it only runs in single connection mode. For better or worse, applications will sometimes perform another query while in another transaction, causing deadlock with PGlite. It's fine if you can avoid that in your app, but makes it not work as a general drop-in replacement for existing apps.
The way I'd rather it be looked at, though, is just as a more convenient, "friendly" way to work with Postgres on the CLI. So maybe it's not for Postgres experts.

In England specifically, most people up to around 1700 or so ate bread made from mixed flours (wheat, rye and barley) raised with what is now called a sourdough starter. Search for 'maslin' loaf for recipes All grains would be stone ground.
The rich people had manchet bread, pure wheat, sieved well and raised with yeast from beer. So ironically less nutrition, but they had more meat &c.
North of the border, oats were important as wheat grew less well at the higher latitudes.
Earlier still in Saxon times (~9th century) people had gruels and porridges made of the mixed grains boiled with water and some meat fat.
